stdin.prompt: Compare the candidate jointly against the frozen reference-only inventory and supplied photographs at the catalogue finish floor. Account explicitly for every core trait using its exact trait ID, citing render and reference evidence. Pass requires a supported match, fail a defining mismatch, unknown missing/clipped/ambiguous evidence. Do not silently dismiss a core reference trait as non-photorealism or downgrade an uncertain trait. Distinguish optional refinement and acceptable variation from defining reference character. Inventory statements are attributed interpretations, not infallible facts: if contradicted or unassessable, report unknown with grounds. Keep observations separate from causal hypotheses; no particular mechanism is required. Relative improvement is not absolute readiness. A clean candidate can pass with supported evidence for every core trait and no blockers. Give every finding and defect a trait_id: the exact inventory trait ID it concerns, or null when it concerns none. The traits listed in known_gaps are known gaps the generator cannot draw yet: do not assess them, and give any finding or defect about one its trait_id.

comparison.checklist:
Recognizable mature open-grown European beech (Fagus sylvatica) at established catalogue rendering quality, not photorealism.
Authoritative owner requirements:

quality_anchors.provenance: Established shipped fn9 production preview (as the date palm's config uses it).
quality_anchors.scope: Stylistic/finish quality floor only, not species morphology.

observations: Only one reference is supplied (reference-0, whole-tree view). No other photos are available to compare against, and no specimen relationship can be assessed.
The photo is a distant whole-tree view, so bark texture, leaf shape, buds and fruit cannot be resolved and stay uncertain.

The strongest visible recognition cues are: pale grey trunk with even tone, a clear straight bole, a V-fork into two co-dominant leaders, a broad domed crown, and fine layered twig sprays at the crown edge.
Leaf colour looks like fresh leaf-out. This is treated as seasonal or lighting variation, not a defining trait.
Other deciduous and conifer trees and wooden frames in the background are not part of the target and are ignored.
Possible causes (open growth, seasonal state, moss at the trunk base) are noted separately as uncertain and are not presented as observed facts.

traits.observation: The trunk is pale silvery grey and looks even-toned, with no deep furrows or plates visible. At this distance the bark texture cannot be resolved, so smoothness is only inferred from the uniform tone and outline.

There is one straight, fairly slender bole with no major branches for roughly the lower 40% of the tree's height, from the ground to about the fork. The only exception is a short, bare, horizontal branch or stub on the left side just below the fork.

The bole splits into two main ascending leaders in a narrow V at about 40-45% of the tree's height. The left leader bends and kinks slightly. Both leaders divide repeatedly into ascending, then outward-spreading, scaffold limbs.

The crown is broad and dome-shaped to flat-topped, and much wider than the trunk's clear height. It occupies roughly the upper 55-60% of the tree and is about as wide as the crown is tall, or slightly wider. The outline is rounded and scalloped rather than conical.
Dark limbs, visible through the foliage, rise steeply from the fork and then fan outward. Toward the crown edge they arch to near-horizontal and slightly droop, especially on the right side.
Leaves sit in fine, flat-to-drooping sprays along slender twigs. This gives the crown edge a feathery, lacy, layered texture, with individual spray tips standing out against the sky.
The crown is fairly open. Sky and the internal branch structure show through across much of it, and the foliage looks like many small clusters rather than one solid mass.
The foliage is a bright, light yellow-green, consistent with fresh seasonal leaf-out. Other seasons or lighting could legitimately show different colours.
Individual leaf shape, margin and venation cannot be resolved at this viewing distance, so no leaf-level traits can be confirmed.
The base of the trunk flares slightly and looks darker, possibly from moss, staining or shadow. The cause cannot be determined.

Lower right of the trunk, below the fork, hanging foliage and branches descend toward the ground. It is unclear whether they belong to this tree (epicormic growth or long drooping limbs) or to another tree behind it.
The crown is somewhat asymmetric. The right side extends further outward and lower, with drooping sprays, and the left side is more compact and higher.

The tree stands alone on an open grassy slope, and its crown is fully developed on all visible sides. Growing space may explain the broad crown shape, but this is only a possible cause, not something the photo shows.
